title: Metrics & Diagnosis: A Feature's Engagement Dropped
prompt: You're the PM for the 'Groups' feature in a large social app. Daily messages sent in Groups dropped 15% week-over-week. The eng and data teams are looking at you. How would you define the right metrics for this feature and figure out what happened?
blurb: A metrics + diagnosis case — define the feature's success metrics, then run a structured root-cause investigation of a sudden drop.

rubric.label: Metric definition
rubric.description: Defines a sensible metric framework for the feature — a primary success metric tied to the feature's goal, plus input/engagement, quality, and guardrail/counter metrics — not just the one number that moved.

rubric.label: Structured diagnosis
rubric.description: Runs a MECE root-cause investigation: is the drop real (instrumentation/logging), internal (a release, experiment, or dependency), external (seasonality, a competitor, an event), and which segment/dimension is it concentrated in.

rubric.label: Hypothesis prioritization
rubric.description: Forms hypotheses and prioritizes which to check first by likelihood and ease of ruling out, rather than checking everything at random.

rubric.label: Quantitative reasoning
rubric.description: Decomposes the 15% drop by dimension (platform, geo, cohort, new vs existing, funnel step) to localize it, and reasons about magnitude and whether it's within normal variance.

rubric.label: Judgment & next steps
rubric.description: Distinguishes symptom from root cause, knows a metric drop can be good or benign, and lands on a concrete next action (rollback, fix, monitor, or escalate).

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Explains the framework and investigation clearly and calmly, signposts, and adapts as evidence comes in.

reference.scenario: Diagnostic + metrics case. 'Daily messages sent in Groups' fell 15% WoW. There is no single right cause — the interviewer evaluates the metric framework and a disciplined, MECE diagnosis. Plausible causes to steer toward if the candidate localizes well: (a) a release regression — a recent app update broke the 'send' button on Android, so the drop is concentrated on Android and at the compose/send funnel step (a real, actionable cause); alternative branches the interviewer can also run: a logging/instrumentation change undercounting messages (the drop is not real), a change that moved users to a different surface (e.g. Groups content now shown in the main feed, so engagement shifted, not lost — a benign/good drop), or seasonality/an external event. A strong candidate defines metrics first, then narrows by dimension to localize the drop before naming a cause, and treats the number as a symptom.
model_points: Clarify the feature's goal and what the metric represents before reacting: what is Groups for (connection, retention?), and is 'daily messages sent' even the right north-star, or an input metric?

Lay out a metric framework: primary/north-star (e.g. weekly connected groups, or retained group participants), input/engagement metrics (messages sent, active senders, groups active), quality metrics (message read/reply rate, meaningful interactions), and guardrails/counter metrics (spam reports, notification opt-outs, overall app DAU so you don't optimize Groups at the app's expense).

Reframe the 15% drop as a symptom and run a MECE diagnosis: (1) Is it real? Check instrumentation/logging changes and data-pipeline issues first. (2) Internal causes: recent releases, A/B experiments, infra incidents, a changed dependency or surface. (3) External causes: seasonality, holidays, a competitor, a news event.

Localize by decomposing the drop across dimensions: platform (iOS vs Android), app version, geography, user cohort (new vs existing, power vs casual), and funnel step (open Groups -> compose -> send). A concentrated drop points to a cause.
Prioritize hypotheses by likelihood x ease of checking — a recent release is fast to confirm via version/platform cuts, so check that before slow external theories.
Distinguish symptom from root cause and judge whether the drop is bad, benign, or good — e.g. if engagement simply moved to another surface, total value may be unchanged.
Land on a next action tied to the finding: roll back or hotfix a regression, correct instrumentation, keep monitoring if within variance, or escalate with a clear readout.

probes.question: Before theories — is this drop even real? What would you check first to rule out measurement error?
Is messages-sent the right success metric for Groups, or an input? What would your primary metric and guardrails be?
How would you narrow this down fast? What dimensions would you cut the 15% by to localize where it's happening?
It's concentrated on Android and at the send step after a recent release. What's your hypothesis and your next move?

probes.trigger: candidate assumes the drop is bad
probes.question: Could a 15% drop in messages actually be fine or even good? Under what scenario, and how would you tell?
You have five hypotheses and limited time — which do you check first and why?

red_flags: Panics and guesses a root cause before verifying the drop is real
Fixates on the single metric that moved with no framework (no guardrails, no quality metrics)
Unstructured hypothesis dump with no MECE breakdown and no prioritization
Never decomposes by dimension to localize the drop
Assumes any drop is automatically bad; misses that engagement may have shifted or the metric is mis-instrumented
No concrete next action or escalation plan
follow_ups: You confirm it's an Android send-button regression from last week's release. Roll back, hotfix, or ship forward — how do you decide, and what do you tell leadership?
If the data instead showed the drop is uniform across every platform, version, and geo, what would that suggest?
How would you set an alerting threshold so you catch a real regression but aren't paged on normal weekly variance?
Suppose messages dropped 15% but time-in-Groups rose — how do you reconcile that, and which metric do you trust?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong candidate resists guessing and first frames the feature's goal, questioning whether 'messages sent' is the north-star or just an input, then sketches a metric framework: a primary metric (retained/connected group participants), engagement inputs (active senders, active groups, messages), quality (reply/read rate, reported spam), and guardrails (notification opt-outs, overall app DAU). They treat the 15% as a symptom and run a MECE diagnosis — first ruling out instrumentation/logging changes ('is it even real?'), then internal causes (recent releases, experiments, infra, a surface change), then external (seasonality, events). Crucially they localize by decomposing the drop across platform, app version, geo, cohort, and funnel step, prioritizing the fast checks (version/platform cuts) first. Finding the drop concentrated on Android at the send step right after a release, they hypothesize a regression, and their next action is to confirm via the release, roll back or hotfix, and give leadership a crisp readout. They note explicitly that a drop can be benign or good — if engagement merely shifted to another surface — and would verify total value before declaring an emergency.

interviewer_notes: Two skills in one: metric definition and structured diagnosis. Make the candidate define a metric framework before they diagnose — many jump straight to root-cause theories. The single most important behavior is checking 'is the drop real?' (instrumentation) before external theories, and localizing by dimension rather than guessing. Steer via probes: once they start cutting the data, reveal it's Android-only at the send step after a release and see if they reach 'regression -> roll back.' Reward the insight that a metric drop can be benign or good. Penalize panic, single-metric tunnel vision, and unprioritized hypothesis dumps. Close on the rollback-vs-hotfix judgment follow-up.
